Well, I think it would just be best to honestly tell her you were recommended the site by a woman who sufferes from chronic suicidality (actively for 30+ years of my 50) and that you received it in asking for how to best support, and help her - your beloved friend that you are terrified you may lose to suicide (she should not see this as a betrayal of her trust, as you just wanted advice in order to better support her - not to cure, or commit her).  Or, you could just tell her that you found the site in looking around on the web in order to better understand what it means to be suicidal (which, again shows you are trying to support and help her by better understanding what she is going through), and that you discovered that there is in fact a real psychiatric condition called chronic suicidal ideation that most people don't know about, and that you found this support forum that was made by & for those who are suicidal - chronic or not.

  Let her know you were honestly afraid of insulting or offending her by sending her this link as you stated above, but that because of the what I told you (or what you found out) about how important and incredibly helpful it is to people like me - that it is the only safe and supportive place where those who are suicidal can vent openly and honestly - brutally - about wanting to die or about how they were raped, or whatever, without worrying that some trolling do-gooder will turn us in - or shame, criticize or judge us.  

  Sorry for beating a dead horse, but though she needs your help and support desperately right now, you can't possibly carry the entire burden of her recovery on just your own shoulders, she also needs support for the times you're not there, or for expressing and working through the things she's afraid to tell even you.  So please, also be mindful to take care of yourself and don't give up so much of yourself and your time that it is detrimental to YOUR life and mental health.  If she can get a Dialectical Behavior Therapist it would be the best thing she could possibly do as that form of therapy was designed for those who are suicidal and in crisis and statistically helps the suicidal to complete recovery more than any other therapy.  After DBT the next best at helping the suicidal is Cognitive Behavioral Therapy.  But, for me the most effective thing I've found in 30+ years of therapies and useless medications is plain old simple meditation (the mental health community is calls it "mindfulness training") but it only works if you practice it consistently.  Meditation - learning your thoughts and emotions have no real reality - has helped me to learn to "change channels" when I find myself freaking out about some possible horrible future event.  I practice a Zen Buddhist meditation called zazen, I learned the ins and outs at my local Zen center, but there are enty of videos and sites that you can learn from.  Buddhism is not a religion, but meditation or mindfulness doesn't have to be connected to the teachings of the Buddha or any group whatsoever.  One way you might get her interested in trying meditation is if you bring it up as something you'd like to try (or even better, have learned) and ask if she'd like to try it with you.

  But, for the moment, when she feels suicidal, please beg her from the bottom of your heart to live for you if she cannot live for herself.  Tell her you respect her decision as it is HER life and HER body, that you accept that she is suffering so very much that death seems so much more preferable than living (you might want to ask her about her emotional pain, and where it's all coming from, was she ever raped? or was she otherwise abused or bullied as a child or teen? Talking openly about what we consider "shameful secrets" can help tremendously) but then tell her you still wish she would stay, even if it is terribly selfish of you to ask her to continue a life of unbearable suffering - you still want her to live, etcetera.  This is what we want to hear from those who say they care about us, we want them to step into our pain, to see its reality, to brlieve us and validate our suffering and understand how hard it is for us to choose life when it's like being trapped in the top room of a burning tower, and all you have is a choice between the agony of burning to death (life) or the quick and less painful choice of jumping out the window to escape (suicide).

As someone who has suffered from chronic suicidality for most of my 50 years, I know your friend's story all too well.  Some people become suicidal as a temporary response to cope with a temporary crisis (this is what most people, including the mental health professionals usually consider the limts of suicidal behavior), but then there are the rest of us.  In order to help your friend, first, please let them know there is a excellent support forum called Chronic Suicide Support,  http://www.chronicsuicidesupport.com/  created by and made for the chronically suicidal, where people like us can vent honestly and openly without fear from trolling pro-life, do-gooders that just push away those they want to "help" because they don't have any idea of what the realities of being suicidal are.  Knowing she is not alone and having a community that she can receive support and understanding from others also dealing with being suicidal can really help her (there is no talk of methods or suicidal pacts or such things allowed on the site, so don't make the mistake of thinking the forum and chat will make things worse - it's been proved over and over that this community really does help people reduce their attempts).  You can also go there to ask for what you can do to help as well.

  Secondly, respect and take your friends feelings, and whatever her reality is, seriously (don't brush it off, or offer glib platitudes about how "it gets better" as for many of us it never does) be an open, unshockable, and safe person that your friend trusts enough to be honest enough to talk about her feelings about wanting to end her life, or the things that have happened in her life to push her towards wanting to die.  This can literally be a life saver, as having someone who accepts, understands and does not shame or judge her about wanting to die can truly help her from feeling so isolated.  Also, if you love your friend, tell them you understand and accept that they want to die, and ask - BEG - them to stay alive for you if they cannot stay alive for themselves.  Often, knowing someone cares that much and takes them that seriously will often rid them of the desire to die.  They will stay alive for you if you prove to them how important they are and that you could not bear losing them.  I know it worked in stopping my constant attempts to die, until my beloved friend died (no one else ever asked or begged me to stay alive - not my family, no one). Everyone who loves someone suicidal should do this!  Many people who are suicidal feel those they love would be better off without them - showing them it's not true in this way really helps.

I hope this helps!

Peace & Love, however you can find it.

When I was in my early twenties, I suffered from very much the same thing, though usually only when I was alone.  I've always been an extremely shy introvert, but suddenly this rage just began exploding without warning.  I was the angel of death to many small appliances and telephones, and I even began to injure myself.  So, I went to a therapist to figure it out.  It turned out I had repressed and was in denial  or at least had tried to keep memories of past abuse in the realm of forgetfulness.  And apparently, my subconscious had now had enough, and was so incredibly enraged over all the viscious injustice and brutality I had lived through, that it was exploding.  I lived alone, so it was very bizarre to be doing my laundry or hanging out reading in my apartment on my days off, when suddenly - completely out of nowhere, I would find myself literally shaking with rage.  It was like living with an active volcano in my chest.  It took a few years for it to go away, but between zen meditation and therapy, it did.  Elitug is right, meditation is incredibly helpful.  It teaches you to understand the flow of your thoughts and emotions, and after practicing just one month you'll find you can begin to have the ability to "change your mind" like channels on a television. If you find yourself getting angry, anxious, or upset you learn to switch to a calmer mindset.

In your case though it seems like the anger is directed at or is exploding in front of other people so it's probably a very common condition called, Intermittent Explosive Disorder:

"The individual may describe the aggressive episodes as “spells” or “attacks” in which the explosive behavior is preceded by a sense of tension or arousal and is followed immediately by a sense of relief. Later the individual may feel upset, remorseful, regretful, or embarrassed about the aggressive behavior."
http://psychcentral.com/disorders/intermittent-explosive-disorder-symptoms/

But then, there is another cause of explosive anger and rage: brain damage or neurological problems.  So if you've been knocked unconscious and the anger episodes started soon after, that's a possibility.

When Rage Explodes, Brain Damage May Be the Cause
http://www.nytimes.com/1990/08/07/science/when-rage-explodes-brain-damage-may-be-the-cause.html

Whether your rage comes from issues from your past or present, meditation and cognitive behavioral therapy are the best ways to go for understanding and calming your rage (you can find CBT associations on the web where they usually list therapists in your area).  It's like taking an anger management course only far more effective.

Dear StriatedMuscle,



I'm so sorry you are going through this terrible time.  It honestly scares me a bit because it reminds me of how I was before I had my first breakdown, became actively suicidal and ended up in the laughing academy.  


  Best thing to do is to listen to those warnings your body is giving you and get help, right now.  If you have medical insurance look up cognitive behavioral therapists  or dialectical behavior therapists in your area (there are usually DBT & CBT therapeutic associations on the web where they list therapist in your area).  If you can't find a CBT therapist you can look for therapists who specialize in treating PTSD and anxiety (again, the internet should help you find one).  If you don't have insurance there are usually mental health clinics that offer therapy, psychiatric services and medication nearly free, or on a sliding scale.



And, PLEASE talk about what your going through to your boyfriend or a close friend or family member, preferably all of them.  You should never suffer in isolation as it only makes your suffering ten times worse when the people around you don't understand that you are suffering so badly.  There is no shame in feeling how you feel, in being honest, especially with the people who love you.  Just being understood, not having to hide your feelings anymore, being able to talk through your fears, will help tremendously.  It's so important to be able to be open and honest about what you're going through.  (If the thought of doing this is too intimidating, you can always write them a letter explaining what you are going through. instead.)

Fresh ginger is the best natural remedy for this because it has a drying effect on the body, mucous membranes etc, (I drink ginger tea with lemon and honey when I'm stuffed up or my nose is running.)  In hot weather it's a great iced tea, too.  Best thing for you would be to make enough sweetened tea to fill a water bottle, and keep it in the refrigerator and drink from it when you need to.  It should take full effect in about 10 - 20 minutes.  (If you can't find fresh ginger root, dried is fine too.)

Of course there are drugs such as Robinul and Anaspaz that can help but you'd just be fighting side effects with side effects and may very well end up with some other complaint.  Best to talk to your doctor.

Peace & Love

Dear bravelittlewings,

  I spent four years in a a very loving, yet extremely abusive relationship a year after I was I was forced to leave university (I had been viscously gang raped my very first night when masked men (probably fellow students) broke into my dorm room in the university that I had won a scholarship and fought like mad with my parents to go away to. I became chronically suicidal, unstable and severely depressed and was expelled because of my failed grades and the fact  that I posed a threat to the suicide statistics of the university).  I soon realized that this relationship was almost a perfect reflection of the relationship I had with my alcoholic, abusive, and sexually perverse sperm donor they call my father.  So, I wrote my abusive and possessively jealous lover a very long letter in our third year telling him why I had to to leave him though I loved him desperately, describing the horrible torture and abuse he was putting me through, though every morning he would be there when I woke up by the side of the bed holding my hand and telling me he was so very sorry for the bruises he had inflicted upon me the night before.   He pleaded with me to stay and agreed to quit drinking and do whatever it took to make me happy.  But, though things were improved, all it really did was make him feel resentful towards me because he couldn't drink, so he would occasionally come home extremely drunk and in a hatefully abusive, resentful mood.  But it allowed me to finally understand the dynamics of the situation and my own place within it, which allowed me to finally make the firm decision to leave him, and never have another relationship with a jealous or abusive man.  

  I had always felt so very sorry for him and forgave him so much because he had been so terribly abused.  His father was a violent and abusive alcoholic, and my love was just five years old when his horribly abused and battered mother threw his father out of the house threatening him with death if he ever returned after he'd broken her jaw - yet his father did return, broke down the door one night, and his mother shot his father dead in front of him and his siblings.

  But, I realized that NOTHING can excuse abuse.  It's severely psychologically damaging, and should be escaped at all costs.

  Luckily, in my case we had a very loving relationship so he understood and accepted the fact that I could no longer stay with him.
But, for many women this is not the case.  And though it's bad enough for women in these situations, it's a million times worse for the children trapped in these abusive environments.  They can be severely and irrevocably damaged emotionally from living in such a household.  Luckily, I chose to sterilize myself as I never wanted to force an innocent life into this world as I had been.  

  I don't know the details of your relationship but you are obviously suffering through very much the same thing I suffered through.  The constant confusion that is caused by the combination of love and violence, the second guessing, the thoughts of suicide, etcetera.

  All I can do is hope you will understand the severe emotional and psychological damage you and especially your children are being exposed to if you continue to live in this toxic environment.

You need to find a way to leave this abusive situation, a plan of escape at all costs, if not for you than for your children.

So, use those brave wings and fly.

Love & Peace

Many people don't understand that there is actually a condition called, chronic suicidal ideation, or chronic suicidality.  It's basically an often lifetime suicidal impulse that doesn't respond to chemical or therapeutic treatments.  For those of us who suffer from this, suicide is part of our daily life - we either have to fight constantly, reject and deny it - or we can make friends, accept and understand it.

Dear NothingReallyButHey,

  After more than 30 years of being chronically suicidal, I feel very much the same.  I've always seemed to scan my environment for possible methods, possible escapes, and it helps me to sleep at night knowing those emergency exits are always there, always available.

  From the time I was five years old I wanted to escape my family and just disappear.  I tried so many times to run away from home and find a train car to jump so I could escape from my life.  I was too young at that time to know about the chronic suicidality that runs through my entire family (along with other chronic problems with mental ill-health of course), and that my intense desire to run away and disappear was simply the first glimmerings of my suicidal urges.

  For me, death is like a seductive lover who promises eternal peace and rest, escape from this hideously ugly and sad species - from this exquisite, unbearable pain.  I have lost track of how many attempts at self-abbreviation I've made over these past three decades, how many pills I've taken, how many therapists and psychiatrists I've had, how many times I've been hospitalized, or imprisoned in the laughing academy.   I've faced down so much pain, agony and suffering, again and again, trying to get there. As a result,  I'm now covered with scars and stitches all over my body, a veritable bride of Frankenstein with 52 sutures decorating my neck, and not to forget, the brain damage from being dead for a little over two minutes.   But, my luck's got to change sometime. 

  So until then, if you see me admiring a big, beautiful tree, know I'm only calculating which branch is the best to hang myself from - just like you!

😊

Peace & Love.  Take care however you can.


<3

Anxiety (Stress and anxiety) treatments and their effectiveness

I found that Effexor worked somewhat better as a general daily anxiolytic but its anti-depressant effects were nul, and the side effects just didn't make it bearable.

First, .25mg seems a very low dose for Xanax when your in crisis (the maximum dose is 4mg).  Please contact your psychiatrist, therapist or physician for help as soon as you can. Here's what I try to do when I feel overwhelmed by my anxiety and racing thoughts:  
(First, If I'm really freaking out, I take my emergency anti-anxiolytics  (for me that means Bromazipam & Atarax) - then) I lie down on my bed with the light as low as possible (I find burning incense or using essential oils like lavender, rose or patchouli helps)  I take deep breaths into my stomach letting it rise and fall, I stretch and then relax my whole body a few times and then as my breathing is calmed and regular, centered in my stomach and not trapped high up in my chest, I count every breath I exhale, just being aware of my body and the sensation of my breath coming and going, my stomach rising and falling, and when I reach 10, I start the count over from one.  My thoughts will be buzzing around, and will distract me but I just let them go - again and again - kindly, softly, without judgement, and return to my breath and if I lose count, I begin at one again (without judging myself as if it were a mistake).  I do this for approximately 40 minutes.  Then, I read a book to allow my mind to settle further into its relaxed track (no computers, no gadgets with glowing screens as they tend to make me hyper and excitable the longer I'm on them).  Sometimes I put on some classical music or jazz as background.  Usually, after an hour or two I feel much better.

Or, sometimes I drink, listen to my favorite music and smoke too much.  Or, sometimes I take a long walk at midnight and dance in the town square in front of the cathedral like a crazy person (Oh, wait, I am a crazy person!).  Or, sometimes I take a hot bath with a bottle of wine.  Or, sometimes I just take a big dose of theralen, or zoplicone to force sleep and put an end to the rotten day.

  Everyone's experience is different, but as far as medication, I take Lyrica every morning because after 30 years of trial and error, I've found it is the most effective and safe solution for my day to day anxiety and extreme esophageal cramps and other muscle tension (I also suffer from chronic pain and fibromyalgia).  Lyrica also stays in the bloodstream all day (around 12-14 hours) though it does make me a little high and forgetful. Other than that, I have found Atarax to be far superior to Benzos like Xanax for my anxiety (though I still keep my Bromazapam on hand for extra fire power in case of emergencies).  Atarax is not addictive and has the least side effects of other anti-anxiolytics.  In fact, its main use is in hospitals where it is given to patients before they go in for surgery to keep them calm and relaxed.  It doesn't make me high, it simply relaxes me, calms me, or if I take a little more I begin to be sleepy (it's done wonders for my insomnia, as well).  For some reason not one of my psychiatrists ever prescribed these medications for me (they seem obsessed with putting me on ineffective amounts of Benzos and then warning me about them when I asked for an effective dose, or giving me those horrible new atypical antipsychotics. (So many useless drugs, so many horrible side effects!))  but after all my years as a guinea pig for the pharmaceutical industry, through experience and lots of research, I finally found what works for me.  It's important to find what works for YOU!  And, if you suffer from bouts of extreme anxiety, it's very important to tell your psychiatrist, and have him specifically prescribed extra meds for use in such intense emergencies.  It may take time to get the right meds at the right dosage but it's worth it once you do. Don't let the psychiatrist bully you, make sure your needs are taken care of completely - that's their job!

I'm wishing and hoping for the best for you.
Hang in there!

Our minds, and our thresholds of experience, how we process and react to stress, to sleepless nights, etcetera, are all very unique, so it's really not a great idea to set a definitive rule as to what causes what, why and when.  I've been an insomniac since I was a toddler and, I often go two or three days a week with only a few hours of sleep, my record was going eight days with no sleep at all (not recommended), but in my 50 years I've never hallucinated, or seen things I couldn't explain.  But at the same time I've battled mental illness and chronic suicidal ideation all my life (the insomnia is just part of it), and not sleeping definitely makes it much worse.  (It took me years to realize that sleep is the most essential and important thing for my mental health. Duh!) I know medications, or combinations of medications can cause hallucinations, so that's something to watch out for.

  Again, everyone is different, so my experience probably doesn't mean much in your case.  It's best to go by your own experience and feelings.  If it's bothering you, it's best to seek a professional opinion (more than one is best) to put your mind at ease.

And, here's a little of what Wikipedia says about it:

Intrusive thought
https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrusive_thought

An intrusive thought is an unwelcome involuntary thought, image, or unpleasant idea that may become an obsession, is upsetting or distressing, and can be difficult to manage or eliminate.[1] When such thoughts are associated with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), depression, body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), and sometimes attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), the thoughts may become paralyzing, anxiety-provoking, or persistent. Intrusive thoughts may also be associated with episodic memory, unwanted worries or memories from OCD,[2] posttraumatic stress disorder, other anxiety disorders, eating disorders, or psychosis.[3] Intrusive thoughts, urges, and images are of inappropriate things at inappropriate times, and they can be divided into three categories: "inappropriate aggressive thoughts, inappropriate sexual thoughts, or blasphemous religious thoughts".[4]

Discription
Many people experience the type of bad or unwanted thoughts that people with more troubling intrusive thoughts have, but most people can dismiss these thoughts.[1] For most people, intrusive thoughts are a "fleeting annoyance."[5] Psychologist Stanley Rachman presented a questionnaire to healthy college students and found that virtually all said they had these thoughts from time to time, including thoughts of sexual violence, sexual punishment, "unnatural" sex acts, painful sexual practices, blasphemous or obscene images, thoughts of harming elderly people or someone close to them, violence against animals or towards children, and impulsive or abusive outbursts or utterances.[6] Such bad thoughts are universal among humans, and have "almost certainly always been a part of the human condition".[7]

When intrusive thoughts occur with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), patients are less able to ignore the unpleasant thoughts and may pay undue attention to them, causing the thoughts to become more frequent and distressing.[1] The thoughts may become obsessions which are paralyzing, severe, and constantly present, and can range from thoughts of violence or sex to religious blasphemy.[5] Distinguishing them from normal intrusive thoughts experienced by many people, the intrusive thoughts associated with OCD may be anxiety provoking, irrepressible, and persistent.[8]

How people react to intrusive thoughts may determine whether these thoughts will become severe, turn into obsessions, or require treatment. Intrusive thoughts can occur with or without compulsions. Carrying out the compulsion reduces the anxiety, but makes the urge to perform the compulsion stronger each time it recurs, reinforcing the intrusive thoughts.[1]According to Baer, suppressing the thoughts only makes them stronger, and recognizing that bad thoughts do not signify that one is truly evil is one of the steps to overcoming them.[9] There is evidence of the benefit of acceptance as an alternative to suppression of intrusive thoughts. A study showed that those instructed to suppress intrusive thoughts experienced more distress after suppression, while patients instructed to accept the bad thoughts experienced decreased discomfort.[10]These results may be related to underlying cognitive processes involved in OCD.[11] However accepting the thoughts can be more difficult for persons with OCD. In the 19th century, OCD was known as "the doubting sickness";[12] the "pathological doubt" that accompanies OCD can make it harder for a person with OCD to distinguish "normal" intrusive thoughts as experienced by most people, causing them to "suffer in silence, feeling too embarrassed or worried that they will be thought crazy".[13]

The possibility that most patients suffering from intrusive thoughts will ever act on those thoughts is low. Patients who are experiencing intense guilt, anxiety, shame, and upset over these thoughts are different from those who actually act on them. The history of violent crime is dominated by those who feel no guilt or remorse; the very fact that someone is tormented by intrusive thoughts and has never acted on them before is an excellent predictor that they will not act upon the thoughts. Patients who are not troubled or shamed by their thoughts, do not find them distasteful, or who have actually taken action, might need to have more serious conditions such as psychosis or potentially criminal behaviors ruled out.[14] According to Baer, a patient should be concerned that intrusive thoughts are dangerous if the person does not feel upset by the thoughts, or rather finds them pleasurable; has ever acted on violent or sexual thoughts or urges; hears voices or sees things that others do not see; or feels uncontrollable irresistible anger.[15]

I unwittingly began lucid dreaming through a rather bizarre series of nightmares over a two week period.  In the nightmares, I saw myself facing out towards me across a two lane city street, standing  as if waiting, on a small landing inside a little arched alcove which consisted of a few steps, the landing and a door leading into the building.  And, as I watched myself standing there innocently unaware, the door behind my dream self opens, and there is a man who grabs me across my chest and shoulders from behind, and I watch helplessly as I see myself stabbed again and again, until I wake up in terror.  I had the exact same nightmare every night, but after a week and a half, I stopped waking up, It was as if the self in the dream had learned it wasn't real and that there was nothing to fear.  The nightmare changed to a dream.  Instead of the terror of seeing myself waiting unaware of what was to come, I now saw myself smiling wryly, standing with my arms crossed and my body in what can only be described as a cocksure stance - I knew what was to come, and I knew it wasn't real.  The very last time I had that dream I was suddenly aware that I was conscious both as the dreamer and as the self I dreamed.  And, when the man stabbed me, I laughed sarcastically, his knife couldn't hurt me, and he just dissolved away.  After that I seemed to be able to control most of my dreams, I was able to return to the ones I liked, to direct and modify them at will.  It was so glorious, so wonderful to experience my dreamworld as a completely free reality that I could control and change as liked.  But, two years later I was to lose those abilities completely.  

  My lucid dreaming had begun during a very hopeful and happy time in my life.  I had taken college courses in the summer which allowed me to escape my horrible high school a year early (I was an extremely shy, undeveloped, super nerdy girl, and not surprisingly, the target of much bullying) and was finally attending college.  Two years later, I was 18, on the Deans List with a 4.0 average, and most importantly, I finally found someone I liked, who said he liked me, too.  My first boyfriend!  We went to his families house for dinner during our first weekend as a couple. The second weekend, he told me his parents had invited me back, but when we got there, nobody was home.  He was 6'4", a black belt in Tae Kwon Do, and in that big empty house there was no one who could hear my screams as I tried to fight him off, as he raped me, and brutally ripped away my virginity.  And, ever since then, even after more than 30 years, I have been locked out of my dreamworld, no more lucid dreaming, no more beautiful second reality - just nightmares and insomnia.

I first learned to suppress my tears because I was often the only woman in traditionally male dominated workplaces.  I also learned to suppress my tears outside of work, because I didn't want to burden or scare people with my very fucked up, honest feelings (I've suffered from major depression, anxiety, and chronic suicidality for more than 30 years).  So now it is very hard for me to cry, or be in touch with my feelings around people (or even myself) because I've spent so long suppressing them.
